section.title: The Baptism of Jesus
section.sectionRationale: Jesus steps out of obscurity and comes to the Jordan to be baptized by John. The sinless One submits to a baptism of repentance, insisting it fulfills all righteousness; and as He rises from the water heaven opens, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. In a few verses the whole Trinity is revealed and Jesus is publicly declared the beloved Son at the launch of His ministry.
section.thesis: By submitting to baptism the sinless Jesus identifies with the sinners He came to save and fulfills all righteousness, and the Father's voice and the Spirit's descent openly declare Him the beloved Son, anointing Him for the mission that now begins.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Jesus comes to be baptized and John objects; Jesus insists it is fitting to fulfill all righteousness; and heaven opens with the Spirit descending and the Father's voice declaring His Son.

units.label: John's objection
units.note: I need to be baptized by You

verses.text: At that time Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.
But John tried to prevent Him, saying, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?”
“Let it be so now,” Jesus replied. “It is fitting for us to fulfill all {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}} in this way.” Then John permitted Him.

units.label: Heaven opened
units.note: the Spirit, and the Father's voice

verses.text: As soon as Jesus was baptized, He went up out of the water. Suddenly the heavens were opened, and He saw the {{pneuma|Spirit}} of God descending like a dove and resting on Him.
And a voice from heaven said, “This is My {{agapetos|beloved}} Son, in whom I am {{eudokeo|well pleased}}!”

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, conformity to God's will and covenant. Jesus is baptized to fulfill all righteousness, fully obeying the Father's plan and standing in the place of the people He came to save; the word looks ahead to the righteousness His whole life and death will secure.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. The Spirit of God descends like a dove and rests on Jesus, anointing Him for His messianic ministry, the promised sign that He is the Servant on whom the Lord's Spirit remains, Isaiah 42:1 and 61:1.

agapetos.gloss: Beloved, dearly loved. The Father's word over Jesus, My beloved Son, echoes the royal Son of Psalm 2 and the chosen Servant of Isaiah 42, uniting kingship and sacrifice; the term was used of an only, cherished son.

eudokeo.gloss: To be well pleased, take delight in. The Father declares His full delight in the Son before a single miracle or sermon, grounding Jesus' whole ministry in the Father's settled love and approval.

basic.context: Jesus travels from Galilee to the Jordan and asks to be baptized by John. John protests, knowing that Jesus has no sins to confess and is far greater than he is. But Jesus insists it is fitting, to fulfill all righteousness. As He comes up from the water, three things happen at once: heaven opens, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice declares Jesus His beloved Son.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the launch of Jesus' public ministry, and Matthew loads it with meaning. Read the baptism not as Jesus needing cleansing but as Jesus identifying with sinners and obeying the Father. The threefold revelation, Son in the water, Spirit descending, Father speaking, is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels onto the triune God.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is baptized to fulfill all righteousness, to do everything the Father's saving plan requires. The Spirit of God descends and rests on Him, anointing Him as the promised Servant. The Father calls Him My beloved Son, a dearly loved, only Son, and says He is well pleased, delighting in Him before His ministry has even begun.
basic.typology: Jesus' words echo Psalm 2, where God's King is the Son, and Isaiah 42, where the Servant receives the Spirit and the Father's delight. The Spirit descending recalls the dove over the waters at creation and after the flood, hinting at a new creation. Jesus enters the Jordan as the true Israel and the new Adam, beginning again where they fell.
basic.christ: The whole scene is a public declaration of who Jesus is: the beloved Son, anointed by the Spirit, approved by the Father. He is the King of Psalm 2 and the Servant of Isaiah 42 in one person. And by being baptized among sinners, He shows from the outset that He has come to stand in their place and bear their sin.
basic.god: God is revealed as three persons in one act: the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. This is one of Scripture's plainest pictures of the Trinity. The Father's delight in the Son, spoken before any achievement, shows a love that is given, not earned, the very love into which the gospel brings us.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 2:7 calls God's King His Son. Isaiah 42:1 is the Servant on whom God puts His Spirit and in whom He delights. Isaiah 61:1 speaks of the Spirit anointing God's messenger. And 2 Corinthians 5 says Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin for us.
basic.oneStory: At the Jordan the true Son begins the mission the first son, Israel, and the first man, Adam, failed. He steps into the sinners' place, is anointed by the Spirit, and hears the Father's love. Everything the Old Testament hoped for, a King, a Servant, a new beginning, converges here as Jesus sets out to fulfill all righteousness and save His people.

context.literary:
The scene is only five verses, and Matthew builds it as a three-step exchange: a request, a reply, and an answer from heaven. The movement of the verbs shows the structure. Jesus 'came' from Galilee 'to be baptized', verse 13; John tries to prevent Him and then 'permitted' Him, verses 14 and 15; and when Jesus 'went up' from the water, the heavens open, verse 16. Nothing happens in the water itself. Matthew skips the act of baptism in a participle, 'As soon as Jesus was baptized', and puts all his weight on what comes after it.

The only dialogue before the voice is the exchange between John and Jesus, and these are the first words Jesus speaks in the Gospel. They are about righteousness and about what is fitting. The first words of the Messiah's public life are an assertion that this obedience, humbling as it looks, is the right path. It sets up the whole Gospel's account of a King who rules by submitting to the Father's will.

Matthew alone gives this exchange. Mark and Luke record the baptism and the voice, and the Fourth Gospel records John's testimony about the Spirit, but only Matthew preserves John's objection and Jesus' reply, and he shapes the voice differently. Where Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 have the voice speak to Jesus, 'You are My beloved Son', Matthew's voice speaks about Him: 'This is My beloved Son'. The declaration is addressed to the onlookers, in the same form as at the transfiguration, Matthew 17:5.

The passage closes the opening of the Gospel and begins the ministry. The first section of Matthew, 1:1 to 4:16, sets out who Jesus is: His descent from David and Abraham, His birth, His preservation, His forerunner, and now His Father's own word over Him. The temptation follows at once, and its two key tests begin with the words 'If You are the Son of God', Matthew 4:3 and 4:6, which put to the test the very title the Father has just given.
context.historical:
The baptism took place at the Jordan, in the southern part of the valley, in the wilderness region where John was working. The trip from Galilee was a journey of several days on foot, so Jesus' arrival is a deliberate act, not a chance encounter. Luke places the event when Jesus was 'about thirty years old', Luke 3:23, the age at which a priest began service, Numbers 4:3, and, as the Old Testament notes, the age at which David began to reign, 2 Samuel 5:4. Matthew does not draw attention to the age, but the correspondence is available to a reader who knows the pattern.

John's baptism was a baptism 'for repentance' in the context of confession, Matthew 3:6 and 11. In that setting the crowd was made of Israelites who accepted that they needed cleansing and a new start before the coming of the kingdom. For Jesus to come into the line, among tax collectors and soldiers, was to be seen in the company of those confessing sin. The early church felt the difficulty. John's own objection in verse 14 shows it, and the Gospel writers do not hide it, which is a mark of authenticity: a church inventing a story would hardly have made the Messiah appear as a penitent.

The setting is also political. John's movement was drawing crowds, and the authorities were watching. Josephus, writing later, says that Herod Antipas feared John's influence. For Jesus to submit publicly to John's baptism was to align Himself with a movement that Jerusalem's leaders already distrusted, and Matthew later has Jesus ask the chief priests whether John's baptism was 'from heaven or from men', Matthew 21:25.

Matthew's scene is also a public one. The crowds are at the river, John is present, and the voice says 'This is My beloved Son', in the third person, so that the declaration is made in the hearing of witnesses. In a society that prized public honour, an open word of approval from the highest possible source gave Jesus a standing that no human authority could give or take away.
context.canonical:
The scene is dense with Old Testament echoes, and each one adds a layer. The opened heavens recall Ezekiel 1:1, where 'the heavens opened and I saw visions of God', and the cry of Isaiah 64:1, 'If only You would rend the heavens and come down'. Matthew's passive verb, 'were opened', suggests that God Himself opens them, and the prayer of Isaiah is, in this scene, answered.

The voice combines two texts. 'My beloved Son' echoes Psalm 2:7, where the LORD says to His anointed king, 'You are My Son', and also Genesis 22:2, where God tells Abraham to take 'your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love'. 'In whom I am well pleased' draws on Isaiah 42:1, 'My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights', which Matthew himself quotes in full in Matthew 12:18 to 21. The voice thus joins a king, a sacrificial son and a servant in a single sentence.

The Spirit's descent and resting recalls Isaiah 11:2, 'The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him', and Isaiah 61:1, 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me'. Jesus will read the second text in the synagogue at Nazareth and say, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing', Luke 4:18 to 21. Peter sums it up in Acts 10:38: 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power'.

The Gospel's later references loop back. The Father's words are repeated at the transfiguration with the addition, 'Listen to Him!', Matthew 17:5. Jesus' own sense of the baptism as the start of a road to death surfaces when He speaks of 'a baptism to undergo', Luke 12:50, and asks the sons of Zebedee whether they can 'be baptized with the baptism I will undergo', Mark 10:38. The Christian practice of baptism in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, Matthew 28:19, takes its shape from this scene.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew's first task is to answer a scandal. If Jesus is the Messiah and the sinless Son, why is He in the line of penitents at the Jordan? The answer he gives is in Jesus' own words: this is 'fitting', and it fulfils 'all righteousness'. Matthew does not suppress the difficulty, and he makes the reply part of the story, so that readers understand that Jesus' baptism is not a sign of need but of mission.

He also wants readers to hear the Father's endorsement before the ministry begins. The Gospel will show Jesus misunderstood by family, opposed by leaders, and abandoned by friends. Before any of that, the Father speaks. The declaration is not for Jesus' benefit alone, since in Matthew it is addressed to the crowd with the words 'This is'. Readers who follow Jesus are given the Father's verdict in advance and are asked to weigh every later rejection against it.

Finally, Matthew intends the three persons of the scene to be seen together. He does not give a doctrine of the Trinity; he gives a scene in which the Son is in the water, the Spirit comes down, and the Father speaks. Later readers drew out the doctrine from such scenes, and the early church was right to do so.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scene describes something that happened once, at the start of the Messiah's ministry. The opened heavens, the visible dove and the audible voice are not offered as normal elements of Christian experience, and nothing in the New Testament asks believers to expect them at their own baptisms. Jesus' baptism was unique in that it was not for His own repentance, and so it cannot simply be copied.

What does carry forward is the pattern of humility and obedience. Jesus 'fulfilled all righteousness' by doing what the Father asked, even where it looked beneath Him. Believers are called to the same, as Paul says in Philippians 2:5 to 8. The scene also frames Christian baptism, because those who are baptized into Christ are united to Him in His death and resurrection, Romans 6:3 and 4, and are 'sons of God through faith', Galatians 3:26 and 27. The Father's word over Jesus becomes, in Him, a word over those who are in Him, as Romans 8:15 to 17 describes.

It also invites care in how the Trinity is taught from the passage. The scene is a revelation of three distinct persons acting at once, which rules out any teaching that the Father, Son and Spirit are merely three modes or roles of one person who appears in turn. It is not a full account of how the three are one, which belongs to the wider teaching of Scripture.

debates.question: Why was the sinless Jesus baptized?

views.label: To identify with sinners
views.case: Jesus joins those confessing their sins, and so stands in their place from the start. Isaiah 53:12 says He was 'numbered with the transgressors', and 2 Corinthians 5:21 says God made Him 'to be sin on our behalf'. On this reading the baptism is the first public step toward the cross, and Jesus later speaks of His death as a baptism, Luke 12:50.

views.label: To obey and to model obedience
views.case: Jesus says it is 'fitting' to fulfil 'all righteousness', meaning the whole of what God asks. John's baptism was from heaven, Matthew 21:25, so submitting to it was obedience. He thus gives an example of humility, which He will later call His followers to follow.

views.label: To be anointed and revealed
views.case: Others stress the Spirit's descent and the Father's voice, which mark the baptism as the moment of public anointing for the work of the Servant. John says in John 1:31 that the baptism was 'that He might be revealed to Israel'. The act is a commissioning.

debates.bearing: These are not rivals. Identification, obedience and anointing all appear in the text, and the best reading holds them together: the Servant is anointed for His work precisely by joining the people He came to save.

debates.question: Did Jesus become God's Son at His baptism?

views.label: No, the baptism reveals what is already true
views.case: Matthew has already told the story of His birth from the Holy Spirit, 1:18 to 23, and the name 'Immanuel'. The voice says 'This is My beloved Son', which names a present fact. The orthodox church has always read the scene as a manifestation of His eternal sonship, not an adoption.

views.label: Yes, a new status was conferred
views.case: Some early groups, citing Psalm 2:7, 'today I have become Your Father', read the baptism as the moment God adopted a man who was not Son before. The church rejected this view as inconsistent with the Gospel's own accounts of His birth and with John 1:1 to 14.

debates.bearing: The text speaks of a recognition in public and an anointing for ministry, not of the beginning of His sonship. John 17:24 says the Father loved Him 'before the foundation of the world', and the voice at the Jordan declares in time what has always been.

study.originalLanguages:
The Greek of this short scene is carefully chosen.

John's protest in verse 14 uses a verb of strong resistance, diekoluen, in a form that says he 'kept trying to stop' Him, since the imperfect tense often marks effort that goes on. Jesus' reply begins with aphes arti, 'permit it now', using the verb aphiemi, which means to let go or allow, with the adverb 'now'. The little word 'now' shows that this is a moment for a particular purpose, which will pass. John's resistance gives way in verse 15 with the same verb: 'John permitted Him', aphiesin, so that the same word of release ends the exchange.

The key phrase is in verse 15, 'it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness'. The word 'fitting', prepon, belongs to the language of what is suitable or becoming, and Hebrews 2:10 uses a form of the same word of God: 'it was fitting for God... to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering'. The first word of Jesus in the Gospel and the Hebrews statement about His path share this idea that the way of humility is the fitting way for God's Son. The verb 'fulfill', plerosai, is again Matthew's key verb, here used not for a prophecy but for a righteousness. 'Righteousness', dikaiosune, is one of Matthew's great words, and appears at 5:6, 5:10, 5:20 and 6:33. In Matthew 21:32 Jesus says John 'came to you in a righteous way', or literally in the way of righteousness. The word here covers the whole obedience God requires, which Jesus takes upon Himself. The pronoun 'us' draws John into it as well, as one who shares in the work of making the way.

In verse 16 Matthew writes that 'the heavens were opened', aneochthesan. The verb is passive, which in Jewish usage often avoids naming God as the actor, so that it is God who opens them. The plural 'heavens' fits the Jewish way of speaking of the sky. Matthew then says 'He saw', and the verb is eiden, with Jesus as the likely subject, so the vision is for Him, though Matthew does not say others saw it. In John 1:32 the Baptist says that he himself saw the Spirit.

The Spirit descends 'like a dove', hosei peristeran, and the verb of 'resting', erchomenon ep' auton, 'coming upon Him', picks up the language of Isaiah 11:2, 'The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him'. A dove in Genesis 8:9 'found no place to rest her foot', and the Spirit here finds His resting place.

The voice's key word is agapetos, 'beloved'. In the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 22:2, God calls Isaac Abraham's 'beloved' son, using this word, and the Hebrew behind it carries the sense of 'only', the one and unique son. The related verb in the final phrase, eudokesa, 'I am well pleased', is in the aorist tense, and there the aorist states the Father's delight as a settled fact, without confining it to a moment. Matthew 12:18 uses the same verb in quoting Isaiah 42:1, so the baptism voice and the Servant song are one.

typology.type: Israel through the water, the Jordan crossing
typology.fulfillment: Israel passed through the sea and later through the Jordan to enter the land, Joshua 3:14 to 17, and Paul says they were 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea', 1 Corinthians 10:2. Jesus stands in the Jordan, the river of the second crossing, and comes up out of it to face a wilderness, as Israel did. The correspondence is that the true Son retraces the national story; in the next chapter He spends forty days in the wilderness and answers every test with texts from Deuteronomy. The escalation in Christ is that where Israel's passage through the water ended in grumbling and failure, His ends in a voice of approval. The type falls short in that Israel's crossing was a corporate event, while Jesus' baptism is a representative act that others will share through Him.

typology.type: The anointing of the priest and king, Exodus 29:4 to 7
typology.fulfillment: Aaron was washed with water at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and then anointed with oil poured on his head, Exodus 29:4 and 7. David was anointed by Samuel and 'the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward', 1 Samuel 16:13. At the Jordan Jesus is washed in water and anointed with the Spirit, and Matthew's order of events, water and then the Spirit, mirrors the priestly pattern. The correspondence reveals Him as priest and king together. The escalation is that He is anointed 'without limit', John 3:34, and that He becomes the priest who offers Himself, Hebrews 9:14 'through the eternal Spirit'. The type falls short because the old anointings were repeated with each priest and each king; His is once for all.

typology.type: The beloved son who bears the wood, Genesis 22
typology.fulfillment: God told Abraham to take his 'only son Isaac, whom you love' and offer him, Genesis 22:2. Isaac carried the wood and was spared, and 'the LORD will provide' became the memory of the place. The Father's words at the Jordan, 'My beloved Son', echo the language of that command, and the Gospel's later story lets the echo grow, since this Son will carry the wood of His cross and will not be spared. Romans 8:32 says of God that He 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all', which is the same language of withholding, now fulfilled. The escalation is that Isaac was replaced by a ram while Jesus is the provision. The type falls short because Abraham's act was a test, and the Father's was a gift.

typology.type: The Spirit over the waters and the dove
typology.fulfillment: In Genesis 1:2 the Spirit of God was 'hovering over the surface of the waters' at the first creation, and at the flood Noah sent out a dove which at first 'found no place to rest her foot', Genesis 8:9, and later returned with an olive leaf, Genesis 8:11, a sign that the waters had receded and a new world could begin. At the Jordan, the Spirit descends on Jesus in the form of a dove, over the water, and rests on Him. The correspondence is of a new beginning in which the Spirit is present over water. Peter links the flood to baptism, 1 Peter 3:20 and 21. The escalation is that the Spirit finds a place of rest in a person, and does not leave. The type falls short in the sense that a dove is a sign; the Spirit's own presence is the reality.

study.christ:
The passage shows who Jesus is by showing how He acts before He acts. The first words of the Messiah in Matthew are not a miracle or a sermon but a request to be allowed to join sinners in the water.

Notice what He does. He leaves Galilee, makes the journey, and goes down into the river, where the penitent stood. Philippians 2:5 to 8 describes this movement as the whole shape of His life: He 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death'. The baptism is the first public step in that descent. Hebrews 10:5 to 7 puts the same thought in His own mouth as He comes into the world: 'I have come to do Your will, O God.' Here He is doing it. Romans 5:19 says that 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous', and the obedience Paul has in mind starts here, in a river, with a Man who has nothing to repent of and who stands where the guilty stand.

He is also the One who fulfils all righteousness, so that what the law required and could not produce, He supplies. Romans 8:3 and 4 says that God 'did by sending His own Son' what the law could not do, 'so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us'. In Matthew 5:17 He says He has come 'to fulfill' the Law and the Prophets, and in verse 20 that His people's righteousness must exceed the scribes' and Pharisees'. The righteousness He brings is not only an example to imitate but a gift to receive, which Paul calls 'the righteousness of God' in Him, 2 Corinthians 5:21. At the Jordan the one who will provide it enters the world of those who need it.

He is the beloved Son, the Servant, and the anointed King at once. The Father's voice draws together Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42, two texts that, read apart, point in different directions: a king who breaks the nations with an iron sceptre, Psalm 2:9, and a servant who will not break a bruised reed, Isaiah 42:3. Matthew's Jesus is both, and the combination is the mystery of the Gospel. The Son who is the heir of the nations comes as the Servant who gives His life. Isaiah 42:1 also says that the Servant will bring justice to the nations, and Matthew 12:18 to 21 will draw that out.

And He is the One on whom the Spirit rests, the Messiah in the literal sense of the word, the Anointed. 'Christ' is the Greek form of the title, and the baptism is the point in Matthew's narrative at which the title is given its content. Luke 4:1 says He returned from the Jordan 'full of the Holy Spirit', and Acts 10:38 says that 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power'. All that He does after the Jordan, preaching, healing and casting out demons, is done in that anointing.

The caution is that the scene should not be turned into a picture of Jesus' own cleansing or growth. He is the same Person before and after. The baptism shows what He is and what He has come to do, and Matthew leaves the logic of substitution to be filled in by the cross, where the sinless One will bear sin, as Isaiah 53:5 and 6 says.
study.god:
This is the most compact picture of God in the Gospel, and every part of it is active.

The Father speaks. His voice comes 'from heaven', and what He says is a declaration of love and of delight. He does not give an instruction or a command; He gives a verdict about a person. John 5:20 and 3:35 speak of the Father loving the Son, and John 17:24 says it was 'before the foundation of the world'. The voice at the Jordan is an eruption of that eternal love into the time of the Gospel. That the Father's approval comes before the Son has performed any public work shows something about how God loves: the love is the ground of the work, not its reward. It also shapes how believers understand themselves, since Paul says that we receive 'the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"', Romans 8:15.

The Son is in the water, standing among the guilty. The God of Scripture is not a God who keeps His distance from His people's need. The One who stood in the Jordan is the One of whom Matthew has already said that His name is 'God with us', 1:23. The scene brings out a quality of God that the Old Testament only hints at: His holiness does not prevent Him from drawing near, and in the Son He does so without compromising the holiness. Hebrews 4:15 says that this High Priest was 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin'.

The Spirit descends. He is shown as a person who comes, rests, and anoints. Isaiah 63:10 to 14 recalls how the people 'grieved His Holy Spirit' and yet how God had 'set His Holy Spirit among them' in the exodus, and asks where that Spirit is now. At the Jordan the answer is given: the Spirit rests on the Son and, through Him, will rest on His people.

All three are present at once, and distinct. The Son does not speak to Himself; the Father does not descend as a dove; the Spirit is not the voice. This is why the church could confess one God in three persons, and why Matthew 28:19 can speak of a single 'name' of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Ephesians 2:18 states the pattern of our access: 'through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit.' The scene shows a communion, not a solitary power: the Persons give, receive and delight in each other.

The scene holds together two things that are easily set against each other. God is sovereign and acts alone to open the heavens, send the Spirit and speak, yet He does so for the sake of a Man who obeys. And God is utterly holy, yet He is pleased with the One who stands among sinners. The resolution is in what that Man will do, and the Father's pleasure anticipates it.

For worship, the passage invites us to start where the Gospel does, with God's love for His Son, and to receive from that love our own place. The first thing to know about God is not what He demands but what He delights in, and the gospel is that we are brought into that delight, 'in the kingdom of His beloved Son', Colossians 1:13.

crossReferences.note: The decree to God's anointed king, 'You are My Son', continues with the nations as His inheritance and an iron sceptre. The Father's words at the Jordan take up the first part, and the rest of the psalm tells what the Son's reign will be and why the kings are told to 'kiss the Son'.

God's Servant, 'My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights', receives the Spirit and brings justice to the nations without breaking a bruised reed. Matthew will quote it in full in 12:18 to 21, and the baptism voice supplies the opening lines.

God tells Abraham to take 'your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love' and offer him. The Father's 'beloved Son' echoes that language, and the Gospel lets the echo deepen, because this Son will actually be given up, Romans 8:32.

The Branch from Jesse's stump on whom 'the Spirit of the LORD will rest'. The dove resting on Jesus fulfils this promise to the royal Shoot, and the gifts of wisdom, counsel and strength named in the following lines belong to the Son from this moment.

'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor.' Jesus reads this in the Nazareth synagogue and says it is fulfilled that day, Luke 4:16 to 21. The baptism is where the anointing begins.

The prayer 'If only You would rend the heavens and come down'. The heavens that open at the Jordan answer centuries of this longing, and Mark's stronger word, 'breaking open', makes the connection even closer.

The consecration of Aaron: washed with water, clothed, and anointed with oil on the head. The Jordan scene has the same elements of washing and anointing, and presents Jesus as the great High Priest as well as the King.

The people remember the days of Moses and ask, 'Where is the One who set His Holy Spirit among them?' The Spirit's descent at the Jordan answers the question, and shows the Spirit present again with the new Moses and the new Israel.

God sent His own Son 'in the likeness of sinful man' to do what the law could not, so that the righteous requirement of the law 'might be fulfilled in us'. This is the theology of 'fulfill all righteousness': Jesus' obedience is for His people.

God made 'Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.' It is the exchange the baptism begins: the sinless One stands with sinners so that sinners may stand in His righteousness.

Peter summarises the story: 'beginning in Galilee with the baptism that John proclaimed', God 'anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power', and He went about 'doing good and healing'. The baptism is the apostolic starting point of the ministry.

John's own testimony: he saw the Spirit descend and rest on Jesus, and was told that this was the sign of the One who would baptize with the Holy Spirit. It confirms the event from the Baptist's side and adds the name 'Son of God'.

study.oneStory:
At the Jordan the story of Scripture gathers into a single moment, with a single Man standing in a river. The Bible opens with the Spirit hovering over the waters, and the first man, Adam, is called 'the son of God' in Luke's genealogy, which leads straight to this scene, Luke 3:38. He failed in a garden of plenty. Israel, called God's firstborn son, failed in the wilderness. Here a third Son comes up out of the water, and unlike the two before Him, He hears the Father's pleasure.

The passage answers the question that has run since the fall: who will stand where Adam and Israel could not? Genesis 3:15 promised an offspring of the woman. The prophets called Him a son of David, a servant, and a branch. The long wait seemed to produce no one who could be the man God had in mind. At the Jordan, God Himself says that He has found Him, and His joy in Him is not provisional.

It also shows the form that salvation will take. The righteous Son goes down to the place of sinners; the Father publicly owns Him; the Spirit is given. Every part of that pattern recurs in the Christian life. Believers are baptized into Christ, Romans 6:3 and 4, receive the Spirit, Titus 3:5 and 6, and are called sons, Galatians 3:26. What the Father says of the Son at the Jordan He says over all who are in Him.

The scene sets up the chapters that follow. At once the Spirit leads the Son into the wilderness to face the tempter, who begins with 'If You are the Son of God', Matthew 4:3. After the temptation comes the public ministry, then the cross, where the baptism that He said He had to undergo, Luke 12:50, is completed. The heavens that open here will be opened again, Revelation 19:11, where the Rider is called Faithful and True.

And it points to the end. In the new creation the whole people of God will stand in the Son's own place, with the Father's name on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4, and the Spirit and the bride will say 'Come', Revelation 22:17. The sentence the Father spoke over His Son at the Jordan is the sentence that, through the Son, He will speak over everyone who belongs to Him. The story began in a garden with a man who hid from God, and it ends with a people who see His face.

quiz.q: Why did John at first try to prevent Jesus from being baptized?

options.text: John knew Jesus was greater and sinless, and felt he himself needed to be baptized by Jesus.
options.note: Verse 14 records John's protest that the roles should be reversed.

options.text: John doubted whether Jesus was truly the Messiah.
options.note: John recognized Jesus' greatness; his hesitation was reverence, not doubt about His identity.

options.text: John's baptism was closed to people from Galilee.
options.note: There was no such restriction; John objected because Jesus was greater than he.

options.text: John refused to baptize anyone who had not confessed sin.
options.note: The point is that Jesus had no sin to confess, yet John's objection was about Jesus' superiority, not a rule.

quiz.q: What reason did Jesus give for being baptized?

options.text: It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.
options.note: Verse 15 gives Jesus' own explanation for submitting to baptism.

options.text: To set an example that all His followers must copy exactly.
options.note: His baptism does dignify obedience, but His stated reason was to fulfill all righteousness, not merely to set a pattern.

options.text: To repent of His own sins like everyone else.
options.note: Jesus was sinless; His baptism was not for personal repentance.

options.text: To be initiated into John's community of disciples.
options.note: He came to fulfill righteousness and begin His mission, not to join John's circle.

quiz.q: What happened as Jesus came up from the water?

options.text: Heaven opened, the Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father's voice spoke.
options.note: Verses 16-17 record all three at once, revealing Father, Son, and Spirit.

options.text: The Spirit descended and rested on Him in the sight of the crowd.
options.note: The Spirit did descend, but the fuller answer includes heaven opening and the Father's voice.

options.text: An angel appeared to announce His ministry.
options.note: It was the Father's own voice and the Spirit, not an angel.

options.text: Nothing visible occurred; Jesus simply departed.
options.note: The heavens opened and the Spirit descended with the Father's declaration.

quiz.q: What did the Father declare about Jesus?

options.text: This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
options.note: Verse 17 gives the Father's declaration, uniting Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42.

options.text: This is My chosen Servant who will suffer for many.
options.note: The Servant theme is present by echo of Isaiah 42, but the actual words name Him beloved Son in whom the Father delights.

options.text: This is the prophet like Moses; listen to Him.
options.note: Those words come later at the Transfiguration's echo of Deuteronomy; here the Father declares Him beloved Son.

options.text: This is the King who will conquer Rome.
options.note: The Father declares sonship and delight, not military conquest.

quiz.q: What does the baptism reveal about God?

options.text: The one God as three persons: Father speaking, Son baptized, Spirit descending.
options.note: The scene is one of Scripture's clearest windows onto the Trinity at work together.

options.text: That God the Father dwells in heaven and sends messengers.
options.note: True but partial; the scene reveals the Father, Son, and Spirit together, not merely a distant Father.

options.text: That God rewards Jesus for the ministry He has completed.
options.note: The Father declares delight before the ministry begins; it is grace, not reward for work done.

options.text: That God is a single person who appears in different modes.
options.note: The three are present distinctly at once, not one person in changing modes.

questions: Jesus stepped into the sinners' place at His baptism though He had no sin. How does it move you that your Savior identified with you from the very start of His ministry?
The Father delighted in the Son before He had done any public work. How would resting in God's given love, rather than earning approval, change the way you live this week?
The whole Trinity was present at the Jordan. How does a clearer sight of Father, Son, and Spirit deepen your worship and prayer?
Jesus said His baptism fulfilled all righteousness, glad obedience to the Father's plan. Where is God calling you to obedience that may look unnecessary but honors Him?
The Spirit anointed Jesus for His mission. In what task or calling do you need to depend on the Spirit's power rather than your own strength?

translationNotes.note: Fulfill all righteousness renders a phrase meaning to carry out everything God requires; Jesus submits fully to the Father's saving plan.

The heavens were opened may also read the heavens were opened to Him, and He saw may also be rendered and he saw; the BSB footnotes note both, and John 1:32-33 records John's witness of the Spirit's descent.
The declaration blends Psalm 2:7, the royal Son, with Isaiah 42:1, the beloved Servant in whom God delights, presenting Jesus as both King and Servant.
